title: Bans, Color Lines and Refusals
bigQuestion: When a champion, a court or a nation refused a fight, who gained power over the sport, and who lost it?

story.title: A Film Stopped at the State Line
story.kicker: In 1910 a boxing film became a question for Congress.
paragraphs: On July 4, 1910, Jack Johnson, the first Black world heavyweight champion, fought James J. Jeffries in Reno, Nevada. Jeffries had retired undefeated and came back to fight Johnson. Newspapers had spent months calling him the hope of white America.

Johnson won in the fifteenth round. That night and in the days after, white crowds attacked Black Americans in many cities, and people were killed. Some city governments then banned showing the film of the fight.

Two years later, in 1912, Congress passed the Sims Act. It made it a federal crime to carry films of prizefights across state lines. The law stayed in place until 1940. Its chief sponsor was Representative Thetus W. Sims of Tennessee.

The story shows that a fight can be refused in many ways. A champion can refuse a challenger. A court or a Congress can refuse a film. A person can refuse a government's order. A nation can refuse the ring itself. Each refusal changed who controlled a fighting art.
story.think: Why would lawmakers try to stop a film instead of the fight itself?

sections.title: A Title Crosses the Color Line

lessons.title: Sullivan Refuses a Challenger
lessons.mainIdea: Heavyweight champion John L. Sullivan refused to fight Black challengers, including the respected boxer Peter Jackson.
reading: In the 1880s John L. Sullivan of Boston was the most famous boxer in the United States. As heavyweight champion, he chose whom he would fight. He publicly refused to box any Black challenger, a practice later called the *color line*. He held the title from 1882 to 1892.

Peter Jackson was born in 1861 on St. Croix, then part of the Danish West Indies. He built his career in Australia and was one of the best heavyweights of his time. In 1891 in San Francisco, Jackson fought James J. Corbett for 61 rounds, and the bout was ruled a *no contest*.

Sullivan never fought Jackson. Because a champion controlled his own title, one man's refusal could keep a whole group of boxers from a chance at the top prize. The color line in heavyweight boxing held until 1908, when Jack Johnson finally got his title fight. Jackson died in Australia in 1901.

words.d: a racial barrier that kept Black athletes from competing against white athletes or for certain titles
a ruling that a bout has no winner, often after it is stopped
a fighter who seeks a match against the current champion

look.title: Who Holds the Door
look.text: In the 1880s no commission or federation ruled heavyweight boxing. The champion decided whom to meet. A top Black boxer asks for a title fight. The champion says no, and no body above him can order the match.
look.prompt: How did the lack of a governing body make the color line easier to keep?

check.q: What was the color line in boxing?
choices: a racial barrier that blocked Black challengers
check.why: The color line was a racial barrier that kept Black boxers from title chances.

check.q: Where was Peter Jackson born?
choices: St. Croix, in the Danish West Indies
check.why: Jackson was born on St. Croix in 1861.

check.q: What happened in Jackson's 1891 bout with Corbett?
choices: It lasted 61 rounds and was ruled a no contest
check.why: The San Francisco bout went 61 rounds and ended as a no contest.

lessons.title: Johnson Wins in Sydney
lessons.mainIdea: Jack Johnson became the first Black world heavyweight champion by beating Tommy Burns in Sydney, Australia, in 1908.
reading: Jack Johnson was born in Galveston, Texas, in 1878. By the early 1900s he was one of the best heavyweights in the world, but champions kept refusing him. He followed champion Tommy Burns, a Canadian, across the world to demand a fight. Burns held the title from 1906 to 1908.

On December 26, 1908, Johnson fought Burns in Sydney, Australia. Police stopped the fight in the fourteenth round, and Johnson was named the winner. He became the first Black world *heavyweight* champion, breaking the color line in boxing's top division.

Many white newspapers reacted with anger. Writers called for a former champion to return and take the title back. That campaign led to the 1910 fight in Reno, and the phrase *Great White Hope* came from it. Former champion James J. Jeffries, then retired on his farm in California, became the man they chose.

words.d: the heaviest weight class in boxing, with no upper weight limit
a phrase from the 1900s for a white boxer promoted to take the title from Jack Johnson
the official recognition of a champion in a weight class

look.title: Jack Johnson's Years in the Record
look.cite: Library of Congress; U.S. Department of Justice, Office of the Pardon Attorney
look.prompt: How many years passed between Johnson's conviction and his pardon?

check.q: Whom did Johnson beat for the heavyweight title?
check.why: Johnson beat Canadian champion Tommy Burns in Sydney in 1908.

check.q: Where was Johnson born?
check.why: Johnson was born in Galveston in 1878.

check.q: What did the phrase Great White Hope describe?
choices: a white boxer promoted to take the title from Johnson
check.why: Newspapers used it for a white fighter meant to beat Johnson.

lessons.title: A Conviction and a Pardon
lessons.mainIdea: Johnson was convicted in 1913 under the Mann Act in a case widely seen as racially motivated, and he was pardoned after his death in 2018.
reading: The *Mann Act* of 1910 made it a federal crime to transport women across state lines for what the law called immoral purposes. In 1913 a federal jury in Chicago convicted Johnson under this law. His relationships with white women were at the center of the case.

Johnson left the country rather than go to prison. He lost his title to Jess Willard in Havana, Cuba, in 1915. He returned in 1920 and served his sentence in the federal prison at Leavenworth, Kansas. He died in a car crash in 1946. He had been sentenced to one year and a day.

For decades, historians and members of Congress argued that the case was driven by racism. On May 24, 2018, President Donald Trump granted Johnson a posthumous *pardon*, meaning a pardon given after death. The pardon did not erase the years Johnson lost.

words.d: a 1910 federal law on transporting women across state lines, used to convict Jack Johnson in 1913
an official act that forgives a crime and removes its penalty
happening after a person's death

look.title: A Record With Two Dates
look.text: A court record from Chicago, 1913: guilty. A presidential document, 2018: pardoned. Between the two dates, Johnson went into exile, lost his title, served a prison sentence and died.
look.prompt: What does a pardon 105 years after a conviction say about how people judged the first decision?

check.q: In which city was Johnson convicted in 1913?
check.why: A federal jury in Chicago convicted him under the Mann Act.

check.q: What does posthumous mean?
check.why: Johnson's 2018 pardon was posthumous because he died in 1946.

check.q: To whom did Johnson lose the title in 1915?
check.why: Jess Willard beat Johnson in Havana in 1915.

lessons.title: Reno, July 4, 1910
lessons.mainIdea: Johnson's 1910 victory over Jeffries in Reno was followed by racist attacks in many U.S. cities.
reading: James J. Jeffries had retired as heavyweight champion in 1905 without losing a fight. Under public pressure, he agreed to return and fight Johnson. The bout was first planned for San Francisco, but California's governor blocked it, so promoter Tex Rickard moved it to Reno, Nevada.

On July 4, 1910, Johnson won in the fifteenth round. News of the result spread by telegraph within minutes. In many cities across the United States, white crowds attacked Black people who celebrated, and people were killed. The fight took place in an outdoor arena built for the day.

The violence showed how a single sporting result could carry the weight of a nation's racial *hierarchy*, a ranking of groups by power. Officials who could not reverse the result turned instead to the film of it. A *telegraph* line had carried the news; the film would carry the pictures.

words.d: a system that ranks groups of people above or below one another
a system that sent messages over wires using coded electrical signals
stopped competing professionally

look.title: Why the Venue Moved
look.text: A promoter plans a title fight in San Francisco. The governor of California blocks it weeks before the date. The promoter moves the ring, the crowd and the film cameras to Reno, Nevada, where prizefighting is legal.
look.prompt: What does this move show about the power of state law over boxing in 1910?

check.q: Why was the 1910 fight moved to Reno?
choices: California's governor blocked it in San Francisco
check.why: The governor of California stopped the San Francisco plan, so it moved to Nevada.

check.q: In which round did Johnson beat Jeffries?
check.why: Johnson won in the fifteenth round.

check.q: What is a hierarchy?
choices: a system that ranks groups above or below others
check.why: A hierarchy ranks groups of people by power or status.

lessons.title: The Sims Act of 1912
lessons.mainIdea: The Sims Act of 1912 banned carrying prizefight films across state lines, and it stayed law until 1940.
reading: After Reno, many cities banned showing the Johnson–Jeffries film. In 1912 Congress went further. The *Sims Act* made it a federal crime to transport films of prizefights between states or into the country. Its sponsors were Southern members of Congress.

The law did not ban boxing and did not ban filming a fight. It banned moving the film. Promoters found ways around it, such as filming in one state and showing the film only there. The law was enforced unevenly. Breaking the law could bring a fine or a prison term.

Congress repealed the Sims Act in 1940. By then Joe Louis, a Black heavyweight champion from Detroit, had held the title since 1937. Historians read the Sims Act as a clear case of *federal* power used to control what images of a Black champion Americans could see.

words.d: a 1912 federal law that banned carrying prizefight films across state lines; repealed in 1940
belonging to the national government of the United States
to cancel a law

look.title: What the Law Forbade
look.text: It shall be unlawful to bring into the United States, or to carry from one state to another, any film or picture of any prizefight or encounter of pugilists, meant for public exhibition.
look.cite: Sims Act (1912), U.S. Statutes at Large
look.prompt: Which step did the law forbid: fighting, filming or moving the film? Why might Congress choose that step?

check.q: What did the Sims Act ban?
choices: all boxing in the United States
carrying prizefight films across state lines
check.why: The 1912 law banned transporting fight films between states or into the country.

check.q: When was the Sims Act repealed?
check.why: Congress repealed the Sims Act in 1940.

check.q: Who held the heavyweight title when the Sims Act ended?
check.why: Joe Louis had been champion since 1937.

lessons.title: Houston, April 1967
lessons.mainIdea: Muhammad Ali refused induction into the U.S. Army in 1967, citing his Muslim faith, and lost his title and his license to box.
reading: Cassius Clay of Louisville, Kentucky, won the Olympic light heavyweight gold medal in Rome in 1960. In 1964 he won the world heavyweight title from Sonny Liston. Soon after, he announced he had joined the Nation of Islam and took the name Muhammad Ali.

During the Vietnam War, the government used the *draft* to call young men into the military. Ali asked to be classified as a *conscientious objector*, a person who refuses military service for reasons of religion or conscience. His request was denied. On April 28, 1967, in Houston, he refused to step forward for induction.

Boxing officials acted within days. The New York State Athletic Commission suspended his license, and the World Boxing Association took away his title. In June 1967 a federal jury convicted him, and he was sentenced to five years in prison, though he stayed free while he appealed.

words.d: a government system that requires people to join the military
a person who refuses military service for reasons of religion or conscience
the formal act of entering military service
to ask a higher court to review a decision

look.title: Two Bodies Act
look.text: A champion refuses induction on a Friday in Houston. Within days, a state athletic commission suspends his license and a private boxing association strips his title. No court has yet ruled.
look.prompt: Why might boxing bodies have acted before any court decided the case?

check.q: Where did Ali refuse induction in 1967?
check.why: Ali refused induction in Houston on April 28, 1967.

check.q: What is a conscientious objector?
choices: a soldier who wins a medal
a person who refuses military service for religion or conscience
a fighter who refuses a rematch
check.why: Ali sought this status based on his faith.

check.q: Which title did Ali win in Rome in 1960?
choices: the Olympic light heavyweight gold medal
check.why: Ali, then Cassius Clay, won Olympic gold in Rome in 1960.

lessons.title: Clay v. United States, 1971
lessons.mainIdea: In 1971 the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Ali's conviction in Clay v. United States, after he had lost more than three years of his career.
reading: Ali did not box from March 1967 to October 1970, when he fought Jerry Quarry in Atlanta. Georgia had no state boxing commission, so a city license made the bout possible. A New York court later ordered the state to restore his license. Quarry was a leading heavyweight from California.

On June 28, 1971, the *Supreme Court* ruled in *Clay v. United States*. The justices voted 8–0 to overturn his conviction, with Justice Thurgood Marshall not taking part. The Court found that the government had not properly explained why it denied his claim as a conscientious objector.

Ali lost his first fight after the ban, to Joe Frazier in 1971. He won the heavyweight title back in 1974 against George Foreman in Kinshasa, Zaire. His case is studied as a refusal that cost an athlete his livelihood and was later upheld by the nation's highest court.

words.d: the highest court in the United States
the 1971 Supreme Court case that overturned Muhammad Ali's draft conviction
to cancel a lower court's decision

look.title: Ali's Case by Year
look.cite: Clay v. United States, 403 U.S. 698 (1971); Olympic records
look.prompt: How many years passed between Ali's refusal and the Supreme Court ruling?

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in 1971?
choices: It banned boxing in New York
It ordered Ali into the Army
check.why: The Court voted 8–0 to overturn the conviction.

check.q: Why was Ali's 1970 fight held in Atlanta?
choices: Georgia had no state boxing commission
check.why: Without a state commission, a city license allowed the bout.

check.q: Where did Ali regain the heavyweight title in 1974?
check.why: Ali beat George Foreman in Kinshasa in 1974.

lessons.title: Iceland Bans Boxing, 1956
lessons.mainIdea: Iceland's parliament banned boxing in 1956, and amateur boxing was allowed again only in 2002.
reading: In 1956 the Althing, Iceland's parliament, passed a law banning boxing. The law covered public matches and the teaching of the sport. Supporters of the ban pointed to serious injuries in the ring. The country had become a fully independent republic only twelve years earlier, in 1944, after centuries under Danish rule.

The ban lasted more than four decades. In 2002 the Althing voted to allow *amateur* boxing again. Professional boxing stayed banned in Iceland, so Icelanders who wanted to box for pay had to compete in other countries. That was 46 years after the ban began.

Iceland's ban shows a nation refusing a sport through ordinary *legislation*, a law passed by a parliament. It differs from the Sims Act, which blocked only films, and from a champion's color line, which a single man enforced. It also differs from Ali's case, where a government punished one boxer rather than the sport.

words.d: the parliament of Iceland
competing without being paid
laws made by a parliament or congress

look.title: Three Kinds of No
look.text: No one: a champion refuses to meet a challenger. No film: a law stops fight pictures at the state line. No sport: a parliament bans matches and teaching across a whole country.
look.prompt: Which of these refusals reaches the most people, and why?

check.q: What is the Althing?
check.why: The Althing is Iceland's parliament, which passed the 1956 ban.

check.q: What did Iceland allow again in 2002?
check.why: The Althing allowed amateur boxing in 2002; professional boxing stayed banned.

check.q: How did Iceland's ban differ from the Sims Act?
choices: The Sims Act banned all boxing
Iceland banned the sport itself, while the Sims Act banned moving films
check.why: Iceland banned boxing itself; the Sims Act only blocked films.

lessons.title: Sweden and Norway Say No to Pros
lessons.mainIdea: Sweden banned professional boxing in 1970 and Norway in 1981, while both kept amateur boxing legal.
reading: Sweden had a famous professional champion, Ingemar Johansson, who won the world heavyweight title from Floyd Patterson in 1959. About a decade later, in 1970, Sweden banned *professional* boxing. Amateur boxing, with its shorter bouts, remained legal.

Norway passed its own ban on professional boxing in 1981. Norwegian boxers who wanted to turn professional had to compete abroad. Supporters of both bans cited medical concerns about repeated blows to the head. Norway's law also covered other sports in which knockouts were the goal.

Both countries later changed course. Sweden allowed professional boxing again in 2006, under a licensing system. Norway's parliament allowed professional matches under new rules in 2016. In both cases a state *license* replaced an outright ban. Sweden's new law took effect in 2007.

words.d: competing for pay as a job
official permission from a government to do something under set rules
an official rule that forbids something

look.title: When Three Nations Closed the Ring
look.cite: Althing records (Iceland); Swedish and Norwegian parliamentary records
look.prompt: Which country banned more than just professional boxing, and how many years before Norway?

check.q: When did Sweden ban professional boxing?
check.why: Sweden banned professional boxing in 1970.

check.q: What stayed legal in Sweden and Norway during their bans?
check.why: Both bans covered professional boxing; amateur boxing stayed legal.

check.q: Which Swedish boxer won the world heavyweight title in 1959?
check.why: Ingemar Johansson beat Floyd Patterson in 1959.

lessons.title: From Ban to License
lessons.mainIdea: Across these cases, refusals often ended not in freedom without rules but in a license, a commission or a court ruling that set new limits.
reading: The color line in the heavyweight division fell in 1908 when a Black challenger finally forced a title fight. The Sims Act of 1912 ended by repeal in 1940. Ali's conviction ended by a Supreme Court ruling in 1971. A different body ended each one: a challenger in the ring, Congress and the Supreme Court.

Nordic bans ended differently. Iceland in 2002, Sweden in 2006 and Norway in 2016 each replaced a ban with rules and *oversight*, meaning ongoing supervision by an official body. Headgear rules, medical checks and licenses took the place of an outright no.

Historians compare such cases to ask who held power at each moment: a champion, a Congress, a commission, a court or a parliament. The answer changed over time. A *regulation*, a rule enforced by an official body, was often the compromise. In the 1880s no official body ruled the heavyweight title, but by the 1960s commissions, associations and courts all claimed a say.

words.d: ongoing supervision by an official body
a rule made and enforced by an official body
a government board that licenses and supervises a sport

look.title: Who Held the Power
look.text: 1880s: a champion decides. 1912: Congress decides. 1967: a state commission and a boxing association decide. 1971: the Supreme Court decides. 2006: a Swedish licensing system decides.
look.prompt: Choose two of these moments and explain how the source of power over boxing changed between them.

check.q: What does oversight mean?
choices: ongoing supervision by an official body
check.why: Oversight means continuing supervision, such as licensing and medical checks.

check.q: How did the Sims Act end?
check.why: Congress repealed the Sims Act in 1940.

check.q: What replaced the Nordic bans?
choices: licenses and rules under official oversight
check.why: Iceland, Sweden and Norway replaced bans with rules and licensing.

review.q: Who was the first Black world heavyweight champion?
review.why: Jack Johnson won the title in Sydney in 1908.

review.q: Put these in order: Sims Act passed; Johnson beats Jeffries; Johnson beats Burns.
review.why: Burns in 1908, Jeffries in 1910, and the Sims Act in 1912.

review.q: Who enforced the color line in the 1880s heavyweight division?
review.why: With no governing body, the champion chose his opponents.

review.q: Which case overturned Muhammad Ali's conviction?
review.why: The Supreme Court ruled in Clay v. United States in 1971.

review.q: Which country banned all boxing in 1956?
What did the Mann Act and the Sims Act have in common?
choices: Both were federal laws used against or around Jack Johnson
review.why: Johnson was convicted under the Mann Act, and the Sims Act blocked films of his fights.

review.q: Which body took away Ali's title in 1967?
review.why: The World Boxing Association stripped Ali's title.

review.q: What is the difference between an amateur and a professional boxer?
choices: A professional is paid to compete; an amateur is not
review.why: Professionals compete for pay; amateurs do not.
